crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Predictive coding and technology assisted review cover the use of machine learning to classify documents in large e-discovery matters. The scope includes relevance review, privilege review, issue tagging, and prioritization of documents for human review. It applies to email, attachments, chat, collaboration tools, and other electronically stored information. The goal is to reduce the volume of documents that humans must read while improving consistency and recall compared with keyword search alone.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on document review platforms that combine a search index, a document store, and a model training service. The platform may be hosted in the cloud or on premises, and it must handle ingestion, optical character recognition, deduplication, and near duplicate detection. Compute is used for indexing, for training classifiers, and for scoring new documents as they arrive. Security controls, access logs, and audit trails are part of the infrastructure because the data is often sensitive and subject to legal holds.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with a collection, processing, and a seed set of documents coded by human reviewers. A supervised model learns from those codes and then ranks the remaining documents by likely relevance. Reviewers then examine the highest ranked documents, correct the model, and repeat the cycle, a process often called active learning. Quality control uses statistical sampling and elusion tests to estimate how many relevant documents the model may have missed. The final output is a set of documents and metadata that can be produced to opposing parties or used for case strategy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on defensibility, transparency, and proportionality. Parties often meet and confer about the protocol, disclose the use of predictive coding, and document the seed set, model versions, and quality control measures. Provenance matters because courts and opposing counsel may ask how the system was trained, what data was used, and whether the process was consistent. Privilege review adds risk, since a model that misclassifies a privileged document can lead to waiver concerns. Data protection rules and cross border transfer limits also shape where documents can be processed and who can access them.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward continuous active learning, where the model keeps improving as review proceeds, and toward the use of large language models for summarization and issue spotting. Generative AI may help draft review protocols, explain model behavior, and query document sets in natural language, though validation remains necessary. Chat and collaboration data, audio, and video are becoming more common targets, which pushes platforms to handle multimodal content. The site tracks 147 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, and those numbers suggest that discovery disputes over AI systems and their training data will keep growing. Regulation and court guidance will likely continue to shape how much automation is acceptable without human review.
